rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On al-Zamakhshari’s syntax, this clause coordinates with Abraham’s earlier statement, with the intervening phrase parenthetical; Ibn Atiyya takes the fāʾ as linking the following account and thus favors identifying the kingdom of heaven with this detailed demonstration.
rows.anchor: الفاء في قوله فلما رابطة جملة ما بعدها بما قبلها وهي ترجح أن المراد بالملكوت

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Abraham's people worshiped idols and the heavenly bodies, so he led them through observation to infer that each changing, setting body must have a maker and manager beyond it.
rows.anchor: فأراد أن ينبههم على الخطأ في دينهم وأن يرشدهم إلى طريق النظر والاستدلال

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the star Abraham saw as Venus.
rows.anchor: والكوكب الزهرة، قاله ابن عباس وقتادة،

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid identifies the star Abraham saw as Jupiter; al-Baḥr notes its unusual quadriliteral morphology and pattern.
rows.anchor: أو المشتري، قاله مجاهد والسدي وهو رباعي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent reply to “when night covered him” is “he saw a star”; “this is my lord” is then either an awkward adjective or, more plausibly, a new sentence. Alternatively it is the reply, with seeing as a circumstantial clause.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن جواب لما رأى كوكبا وعلى هذا جوزوا في قال هذا ربي أن يكون نعتا للكوكب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some read “this is my lord” as a reproachful question with the interrogative hamza elided; Ibn al-Anbari calls that elision anomalous because a distinguishing cue is normally needed.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأنباري: وهذا شاذ لأنه لا يجوز أن يحذف الحرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A literal, committed claim that the star is God would contradict prophetic protection from sin and shirk; the childhood-worship account attributed to Ibn Abbas may be unsound, and claims that it happened after maturity are baseless.
rows.anchor: فيستحيل عليه أن يكون هذا الإخبار على سبيل الاعتقاد والتصميم لعصمة الأنبياء من المعاصي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report says Abraham saw and worshiped the star, moon, and sun in childhood before each set; Abū Ḥayyān says the report may not be authentic.
rows.anchor: وما روي عن ابن عباس أن ذلك وقع له في حال صباه وقبل بلوغه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari explains the wording as a fair-minded opponent's quotation of the other side, followed by a proof that invalidates it; this draws people toward truth without partisan disputation.
rows.anchor: هذا ربي قول من ينصف خصمه مع علمه أنه مبطل فيحكي قوله كما هو

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari sees Abraham’s apparent agreement as a stratagem to expose the argument, like his outwardly joining the star-watchers before saying he was ill.
rows.anchor: فيكون هذا القول منه استدراجا لإظهار الحجة وتوسلا إليها كما توسل إلى كسر الأصنام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham rejects worship of bodies that set, change state, move, or disappear behind a veil, since these are properties of corporeal objects.
rows.anchor: لا أحب عبادة الآفلين المتغيرين عن حال إلى حال المنتقلين من مكان إلى مكان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Setting is a clearer proof than rising because it includes concealment; the plural “those that set” stresses that many stars share the trait, leaving this one with no claim to worship.
rows.anchor: وجاء بلفظ الآفلين ليدل على أن ثم آفلين كثيرين ساواهم هذا الكوكب في الأفول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham did not wait for the first star to rise because stars become visible as night darkens; after rebutting it, he awaited the brighter moon and then sun to show they share its createdness.
rows.anchor: أولا ما ارتقب حتى بزغ الكوكب لأنه بإظلام الليل تظهر الكواكب بخلاف حاله مع القمر والشمس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The moon was seen at its first rising, and Abraham repeated the argument with the sun because it is brighter, larger, and more beneficial, yet likewise subject to change.
rows.anchor: ثم عمل كذلك في الشمس ارتقبها إذ كانت أنور من القمر وأضوأ وأكبر جرما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lost people are worshipers of created beings; the verse is therefore used by some to argue that “this is my lord” was literal and occurred in childhood.
rows.anchor: القوم الضالون هنا عبدة المخلوقات كالأصنام وغيرها واستدل بهذا من زعم أن قوله: هذا ربي

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari takes Abraham’s plea for guidance as a warning that anyone who makes the setting moon divine is astray, since guidance depends on God’s enabling grace.
rows.anchor: لئن لم يهدني ربي تنبيه لقومه على أن من اتخذ القمر إلها وهو نظير الكوكب في الأفول فهو ضال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sun is usually feminine, though it can be masculine; here it is feminine first, then the masculine demonstrative follows the less common usage and agrees with the predicate.
rows.anchor: فلما رأى الشمس بازغة قال هذا ربي هذا أكبر المشهور في الشمس أنها مؤنثة.

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says the masculine demonstrative refers to the visible object or luminous body; al-Akhfash supplies “this rising body.”
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عطية: ذكر أي هذا المرئي أو النير وقدره الأخفش، هذا الطالع،

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says the subject was made to match the predicate because both denote one thing, avoiding any hint of feminine marking for God.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: جعل المبتدأ مثل الخبر لكونهما عبارة عن شيء واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation takes “sun” to mean light, which is masculine.
rows.anchor: الشمس بمعنى الضياء قال تعالى: جعل الشمس ضياء فأشار إلى الضياء والضياء مذكر،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan suggests Abraham’s reported speech may reflect a language without masculine/feminine demonstrative distinctions; the Qur’an uses Arabic feminine forms in its own narration, not in the quotation.
rows.anchor: أكثر لغة الأعاجم لا يفرقون في الضمائر ولا في الإشارة بين المذكر والمؤنث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the sun sets, Abraham declares himself free of the celestial bodies his people associate with their creator; with no remaining luminary example, his proof is complete and he openly disowns their worship.
rows.anchor: ولما أفلت الشمس لم يبق لهم شيء يمثل لهم به وظهرت حجته وقوي بذلك على منابذتهم

rows.speaker: الماتريدي
rows.claim: Al-Maturidi says the lights' successive dominance shows they cannot be gods, since a true Lord cannot be overcome and darkness overcomes the sun's light.
rows.anchor: وقال الماتريدي: الاختيار أن يقال: استدل على عدم صلاحيتها للإلهية لغلبة نور القمر

rows.speaker: ابن أبي الفضل
rows.claim: Ibn Abi al-Fadl objects that darkness comes only after the sun has gone, so it did not meet or overpower the sun while both were present.
rows.anchor: ما جاء الظلام إلا بعد ذهاب الشمس فلم يجتمع معها حتى يقال قهرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other commentators infer createdness from the luminaries’ transitions between states; if even these lofty bodies are unfit for divinity, wooden and stone idols are still less fit.
rows.anchor: استدل بما ظهر عليها من شأن الحدوث والانتقال من حال إلى حال وذلك من صفات الأجسام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commentators agree the observations occurred in one night, with disagreement whether the star was Venus or Jupiter; the star set, the moon rose, its light faded near sunrise, and then the sun rose.
rows.anchor: وأجمع المفسرون على أن رؤية هذه النيرات كانت في ليلة واحدة، رأى الكوكب الزهرة أو المشتري

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says this sequence could fit one night only from the fifteenth through the twentieth lunar night, requiring the moon’s near-setting to count as setting.
rows.anchor: وهذا الترتيب يستقيم في الليلة الخامسة عشر من الشهر إلى ليلة عشرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan rejects allegorical recastings of the star, moon, and sun as inner faculties or metaphysical principles as esoteric riddles unsupported by the Arabic sense of the verse.
rows.anchor: وهذان التفسيران شبيهان بتفسير الباطنية لعنهم الله إذ هما لغز ورمز ينزه كتاب الله عنهما

rows.speaker: ابن سينا
rows.claim: Ibn Sina interprets setting as contingency; al-Ghazali says what is contingent needs an effective cause and must ultimately depend on a necessary existent.
rows.anchor: وكان ابن سينا يفسر الأفول بالإمكان فزعم الغزالي أن المراد بأفولها إمكانها لذاتها

rows.speaker: ابن سينا
rows.claim: The Ismaili account ranks the star as the licensed caller, the moon as the deputy or minister, the sun as imam, and Abraham as the respondent.
rows.anchor: اللاحق وهو فوق المأذون بمنزلة الوزير من الإمام والشمس الإمام وإبراهيم في درجة المستجيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan dismisses the Ismaili allegory that maps the star, moon, sun, and Abraham to ranks in a secret hierarchy as confused symbolism with no textual support.
rows.anchor: هذا التخليط، واللغز الذي لا تدل عليه الآية بوجه من وجوه الدلالات

rows.speaker: القشيري
rows.claim: Al-Qushayri allegorizes night, star, moon, and sun as stages of spiritual seeking, rational proof, knowledge, and mystical unveiling, ending in freedom from association.
rows.anchor: قال القشيري: لما جن عليه الليل أحاط به سجوف الطلب ولم يتجل له بعد صباح الوجود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan expresses astonishment that people who regard Sufis as God's elect use such interpretations of scripture.
rows.anchor: والعجب كل العجب من قوم يزعمون أن هؤلاء المنسوبين إلى الصوف هم خواص الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “I turned my face” means directing intention, worship, monotheism, faith, and related devotion to the one who originated the world containing the luminaries.
rows.anchor: أي أقبلت بقصدي وعبادتي وتوحيدي وإيماني وغير ذلك مما يعمه المعنى المعبر عنه بوجهي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse names the heavens and earth as containers for the luminaries and wood-and-stone idols, using the container for what it contains; Abraham is ḥanīf by turning from every religion to true worship and is surrendered to God.
rows.anchor: وحنيفا مائلا عن كل دين إلى دين الحق وهو عبادة الله تعالى مسلما أي منقادا إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After rejecting his father's and people's idols, Abraham uses plain rational evidence they can grasp rather than a scriptural proof requiring disputed premises, then emphasizes his disavowal of shirk.
rows.anchor: ثم استدل على ضلالهم بقضايا العقول إذ لا يذعنون للدليل السمعي لتوقفه في الثبوت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reciprocal disputation concerns God's unity; the opponents rely on inherited custom and threats from idols, while Abraham answers that decisive proof has guided him and their argument is futile.
rows.anchor: والمعنى وحاجه قومه في توحيد الله ونفي الشركاء عنه منكرين لذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan compares the idol-threat to the people of Hud claiming one of their gods had afflicted him; the cited example is a threat of harm from a deity.
rows.anchor: كقول: قوم هود إن نقول إلا اعتراك بعض آلهتنا بسوء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nafi and Ibn Amir, in Hisham’s transmission, read the address with a light nūn; the underlying form has the indicative nūn and the protective nūn, with grammarians disputing which is omitted.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع وابن عامر بخلاف عن هشام أتحاجوني بتخفيف النون وأصله بنونين

rows.speaker: مكي
rows.claim: Makki calls the light reading an ugly, distant deletion that is acceptable in poetry but, he says, unnecessary in Qur'an; Abu Hayyan rejects this criticism and notes it may be a Ghatafan dialect.
rows.anchor: وقول مكي ليس بالمرتضى، وقيل: التخفيف لغة لغطفان، وقرأ باقي السبعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The other canonical readers retain the doubled nūn by assimilation to avoid two consecutive moving identical letters; full separation is possible in ordinary speech but not read here.
rows.anchor: وقرأ باقي السبعة بتشديد النون أصله أتحاجونني فأدغم هروبا من استثقال المثلين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “In God” attaches to the second verb in the reciprocal construction, not the first; the circumstantial clause says they debate despite God's having already guided Abraham, making their case futile.
rows.anchor: وفي الله متعلق بأتحاجوني لا بقوله وحاجه قومه والمسألة من باب الإعمال

rows.speaker: الكفار
rows.claim: The disbelievers reportedly threatened that their gods might afflict Abraham with leprosy or disease because he insulted and belittled them.
rows.anchor: حكي أن الكفار قالوا لإبراهيم عليه السلام: أما خفت أن تصيبك آلهتنا ببرص أو داء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham says the idols have neither power nor independence, so they cannot frighten him; “mā” may mean the things associated with God or those whom they associate with God.
rows.anchor: لست أخاف الذي تشركون به لأنه لا قدرة له ولا غنى عنده

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya treats “unless my Lord wills something” as a disconnected exception: Abraham fears only a harm God wills, not harm caused by powerless idols; al-Hawfi agrees.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية استثناء ليس من الأول ولما كانت قوة الكلام أنه لا يخاف ضرا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari treats the exception as connected to the general times covered by the negation: Abraham fears no idol at any time unless God wills a frightening harm through it.
rows.anchor: إلا وقت مشيئة ربي شيئا يخاف فحذف الوقت يعني لا أخاف معبوداتكم في وقت قط

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abu al-Baqa allows connected or disconnected exception, and for the connected reading takes it from circumstances, meaning “except in the state in which my Lord wills.”
rows.anchor: وجوز أبو البقاء أن يكون متصلا ومنقطعا إلا أنه جعله متصلا مستثنى من الأحوال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Something” is accusative either as an object or as a cognate accusative meaning “a willing.”
rows.anchor: وانتصب شيئا على المصدر أي مشيئة أو على المفعول به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's knowledge of all events explains why a feared harm cannot be ruled out under either reading of the exception; “knowledge” is an accusative specification transformed from the subject.
rows.anchor: وسع ربي كل شيء علما ذكر عقيب الاستثناء سعة علم الله في تعلقه بجميع الكوائن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing question rebukes their heedlessness in worshiping things that neither harm nor benefit, and urges them to consider Abraham’s proof against their divinity.
rows.anchor: تنبيه لهم على غفلتهم حيث عبدوا ما لا يضر ولا ينفع، وأشركوا بالله

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari glosses the question as a call to distinguish sound from corrupt reasoning and the capable from the incapable; al-Razi says denying rivals does not itself entail punishment.
rows.anchor: أفلا تتذكرون فتميزوا بين الصحيح والفاسد والقادر والعاجز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question expresses astonishment at fearing powerless idols while not fearing association with the God who controls benefit, harm, and all affairs; the changed objects avoid equating God with idols.
rows.anchor: استفهام معناه التعجب والإنكار كأنه تعجب من فساد عقولهم حيث خوفوه خشبا وحجارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conjunction links “you do not fear” to “how do I fear,” placing both under the same rebuke; the wording uses “what” because idols are non-rational objects.
rows.anchor: ولا تخافون معطوف على أخاف فهو داخل في التعجب والإنكار واختلف متعلق الخوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Authority” means proof: after rationally refuting the idols, Abraham also denies any revealed evidence for associating them with God, so shirk is invalid both rationally and scripturally.
rows.anchor: والسلطان الحجة والإشراك لا يصح أن يكون عليه حجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reading “sulṭānan” with a ḍamma on lām is either a dialect that establishes this vocal pattern or vowel-following that does not establish it.
rows.anchor: وقرئ سلطانا بضم اللام والخلاف هل ذلك لغة فيثبت به بناء فعلان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham asks which of the two parties, idolaters or monotheists, deserves safety, presenting a known answer as an open question; he avoids saying “which of us” to avoid self-praise.
rows.anchor: ويعني فريق المشركين وفريق الموحدين وعدل عن أينا أحق بالأمن أنا أم أنتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional has an omitted answer: if they are knowledgeable and discerning, they should identify which party is safer.
rows.anchor: وجواب الشرط محذوف أي إن كنتم من ذوي العلم والاستبصار فأخبروني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent speaker of the answer is Abraham: he voices the answer to his own rhetorical question, identifying believers as the party entitled to safety.
rows.anchor: الظاهر أنه من كلام إبراهيم لما استفهمهم استفهام عالم بمن هو الآمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other proposals make the answer Abraham’s people admitting an argument against themselves, or God’s words commanded to Abraham, or a divine verdict separating the disputants.
rows.anchor: هو من كلام الله أمر إبراهيم أن يقوله لقومه أو قاله على جهة فصل القضاء بين خلقه

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Ali is reported to take “those who believe” as Abraham and his companions; another report attributed to him says Abraham alone.
rows.anchor: وليست في هذه الأمة قاله علي وعنه إبراهيم خاصة

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima restricts the believers to those who migrated to Medina; another report takes them generally, which Abu Hayyan regards as the apparent scope.
rows.anchor: أو من هاجر إلى المدينة، قاله عكرمة أو عامة قاله بعضهم وهو الظاهر،

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud and Ubayy identify the ظلم that excludes safety as shirk.
rows.anchor: والظلم هنا الشرك قاله ابن مسعود وأبي

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: When Companions worried that everyone wrongs themselves, the Prophet explained this verse by quoting Luqman: associating partners with God is a great wrong.
rows.anchor: فقال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم:

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: When Umar asked what the wrong meant, Ubayy answered that it was shirk, relieving him; Zayd ibn Suhan and Salman had a similar exchange.
rows.anchor: ولما قرأها عمر عظمت عليه فسأل أبيا فقال: إنه الشرك يا أمير المؤمنين

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid's wording “with shirk” is a gloss on the meaning rather than a canonical reading, since it differs from the written consonantal text.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مجاهد: ولم يلبسوا إيمانهم بشرك ولعل ذلك تفسير معنى إذ هي قراءة تخالف السواد،

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari interprets the wrong as a grave sin that makes a person dissolute, arguing that “mixing” fits sin but not simultaneous faith and shirk.
rows.anchor: أي لم يخلطوا إيمانهم بمعصية تفسقهم وأبى تفسير الظلم بالكفر لفظ اللبس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan calls this a concealed Mu'tazili position: the Prophet explicitly interpreted the wrong as shirk, so that explanation should be accepted over al-Zamakhshari's reading.
rows.anchor: وهذه دفينة اعتزال أي إن الفاسق، ليس له الأمن إذا مات مصرا على الكبيرة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording permits “did not mix” to continue the relative clause or to be a circumstantial clause; Arabic permits a wāw with a negative clause, contrary to claims that it is rare or required.
rows.anchor: ولم يلبسوا يحتمل أن يكون معطوفا على الصلة ويحتمل أن يكون حالا دخلت واو الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ikrima reads the verb with a ḍamma on yāʾ; the clause can have an omitted subject or predicate, while al-Nahhas and al-Hawfi's alternative parsing is remote.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عكرمة: ولم يلبسوا بضم الياء ويجوز في الذين أن يكون خبر مبتدأ محذوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “That was Our argument” points to Abraham’s reasoning from the night’s observation through the declaration of security; the possessive is honorific and uses the majestic plural.
rows.anchor: الإشارة بتلك إلى ما وقع به الاحتجاج من قوله فلما جن عليه الليل إلى قوله وهم مهتدون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The argument was either brought to Abraham's mind as rational proof created within him, or given by revelation and instruction.
rows.anchor: إذ هي من الحجج العقلية، أو آتيناها بوحي منا ولقناه إياها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan rejects al-Hawfi's parsing that makes “We gave it” an adjective of “Our argument”; he also discusses why the phrase “against his people” cannot attach as proposed under other parsings.
rows.anchor: وأجاز الحوفي أن يكون آتيناها في موضع النعت لحجتنا والنية فيها الانفصال

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari glosses “We gave it to Abraham” as guiding and enabling him to discover the argument; a circumstantial parsing can mean it prevailed over his people's arguments.
rows.anchor: آتيناها إبراهيم أرشدناه إليها ووفقناه لها وهذا تفسير معنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammarians differ over the two objects of “We gave it”: al-Hawfi and al-Suhayli take the pronoun first and Abraham second, while the majority reverse them; Ibn Atiyya attaches “against his people” to the verb.
rows.anchor: وأما مذهب الجمهور فالهاء مفعول ثان وابراهيم مفعول أول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The elevated ranks granted to people may mean learning, prophethood, virtue, sincerity, or reward; Abu Hayyan favors argument and exposition because that best fits the context.
rows.anchor: أو بالحجة والبيان، أقوال أقر بها الأخير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Kufan readers leave “degrees” indefinite with nūn; the others annex it, with the indefinite form parsed as an adverb or second object under a verb meaning “grant.”
rows.anchor: ونون درجات الكوفيون وأضافها الباقون ونصبوا المنون على الظرف أو على أنه مفعول ثان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is wise in managing people or allocating them among idolaters and worshipers, and knows their deeds and arguments; the address may turn to the Messenger or honor Abraham directly.
rows.anchor: أي حكيم في تدبير عباده عليم بأفعالهم أو حكيم في تقسيم عباده إلى عابد صنم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Isaac was Abraham's biological son by Sarah and Jacob his grandson through Isaac; the gift of Israel's prophetic line is counted among Abraham's greatest blessings.
rows.anchor: إسحاق ابنه لصلبه من سارة يعقوب ابن إسحاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation says Ishmael is omitted because the passage focuses on the Israelite prophets descended from Isaac and Jacob; Muhammad, the sole prophet from Ishmael, is left out because Abraham's monotheism is the argument to Arabs.
rows.anchor: لأن المقصود بالذكر هنا أنبياء بني إسرائيل وهم بأسرهم أولاد إسحاق ويعقوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan rejects Ibn Atiyya's attachment of “We gave” to “We gave the argument”: the latter has a syntactic role as predicate or circumstantial clause, which the former cannot share.
rows.anchor: ولا يصح هذا لأن آتيناها لها موضع من الإعراب إما خبر.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Each of them We guided” means both Isaac and Jacob were guided.
rows.anchor: كلا هدينا أي كل واحد من إسحاق ويعقوب هدينا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah is named among Abraham's honored forebears, “from before” stressing his antiquity; he was a monotheist even though idol worship began among his people.
rows.anchor: لما ذكر شرف أبناء إبراهيم ذكر شرف آبائه فذكر نوحا الذي هو آدم الثاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah's people urged one another not to abandon their idols, but Noah worshiped God alone and called his people to reject idols, paralleling Abraham's mission.
rows.anchor: وكان إبراهيم عبدت الأصنام في زمانه ووحد هو الله تعالى ودعا إلى رفضها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “From his descendants” may refer to Noah as the nearest antecedent, which includes Lot, or to Abraham as the passage's main subject; Ibn Abbas allows the listed prophets to count through an uncle, whom Arabs call a father.
rows.anchor: قيل: ومن ذرية إبراهيم عاد الضمير عليه لأنه المقصود بالذكر

rows.speaker: أبو سليمان الدمشقي
rows.claim: Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi says Lot was granted as support and assistance.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو سليمان الدمشقي: ووهبنا له لوطا في المعاضدة والنصرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: David and Solomon are paired as father and son, kings and prophets; David comes first by chronology, scripture, and being Solomon's origin.
rows.anchor: وقرنهما لأنهما أب وابن ولأنهما ملكان نبيان وقدم داود لتقدمه في الزمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Job and Joseph are paired for their trials and eventual safety: bodily affliction and abandonment for Job, imprisonment and exile from family for Joseph; Job is first because his trial was greater.
rows.anchor: وأيوب ويوسف قرنهما لاشتراكهما في الامتحان أيوب بالبلاء في جسده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses and Aaron are paired as brothers, with Moses first because he spoke with God.
rows.anchor: وموسى وهارون قرونهما لاشتراكهما في الأخوة وقدم موسى لأنه كليم الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Thus We reward the good-doers” compares Abraham's gift of proof and righteous descendants with the reward given to those who worship attentively.
rows.anchor: مثل ذلك الجزاء من إيتاء الحجة وهبة الأولاد الخيرين نجزي من كان محسنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zechariah, John, Jesus, and Elias are grouped for asceticism; order reflects chronology and parent-child relation, while Jesus precedes Elias because of his scripture and wider following.
rows.anchor: قرن بينهم لاشتراكهم في الزهد الشديد والإعراض عن الدنيا

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Masud identifies Idris as Elias; Abu Hayyan rejects it because multiple reports make Idris Noah's grandfather. Another view identifies Elias with al-Khidr.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن مسعود أن إدريس هو إلياس ورد ذلك بأن إدريس هو جد نوح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The readings differ over lengthening or shortening the name Zakariyya; Ibn Abbas in a variant transmission, al-Hasan, and Qatada ease the hamza in Elias.
rows.anchor: وتقدم خلاف القراء في زكريا مدا وقصرا، وقرأ ابن عباس باختلاف منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Jesus is included in Abraham's descendants, the verse shows a daughter's child counts as descendants; Abu Ja'far al-Baqir and Yahya ibn Ya'mar used Hasan and Husayn's descent through Fatima against al-Hajjaj.
rows.anchor: البنت داخل في الذرية وبهذه الآية استدل على دخوله في الوقف على الذرية،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “All were among the righteous” refers to all fourteen prophets previously named, not only the last four.
rows.anchor: كل من الصالحين لا يختص كل بهؤلاء الأربعة، بل يعم جميع من سبق

rows.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam identifies al-Yasa as Joshua son of Nun; another scholar identifies him as al-Yasa son of Akhtub son of al-Ajuz.
rows.anchor: واليسع قال زيد بن أسلم: هو يوشع بن نون، وقال غيره: هو اليسع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers use al-Yasa with the definite article; the two Kufan readers use al-Laysaʿ on the faʿyal pattern. Grammarians debate whether the name is Arabic or foreign and whether its article is original, added, or removable.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور واليسع كأن أل أدخلت على مضارع وسع، وقرأ الأخوان والليسع

rows.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: A competing view treats al-Yasa as a form of an Arabic verb, while other accounts treat it as a borrowed name; Abu Hayyan discusses the article's morphology under each analysis.
rows.anchor: فأما على قراءة الجمهور وقول من قال: إنه عربي فقال: هو مضارع سمي به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse about a prophet whom the Israelites asked to appoint a king is cited as an alternative setting for identifying Ishmael as an Israelite prophet in Saul's time.
rows.anchor: كان زمان طالوت وهو المعني بقوله إذ قالوا لنبي لهم ابعث لنا ملكا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The four names are grouped because their communities left them no followers; together the prophets illustrate six stations: kingship, severe trial, trial followed by rule, proofs and force, asceticism, and lack of followers.
rows.anchor: وإنما جمع هؤلاء الأربعة لأنهم لم يبق لهم من الخلق أتباع ولا أشياع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The names are foreign and generally indeclinable; al-Yasa declines without nunation and Lot is fully declinable because its middle letter is still and the name is masculine, though Muslims rarely use it.
rows.anchor: وهذه الأسماء أعجمية لا تجر بالكسرة ولا تنون إلا اليسع فإنه يجر بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We favored them over the worlds” establishes that prophets outrank saints and, because “worlds” includes angels, that prophets outrank angels; Ibn Atiyya limits the phrase to the people of their own time.
rows.anchor: فيه دلالة على أن الأنبياء أفضل من الأولياء خلافا لبعض من ينتمي إلى الصوف

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari attaches “their fathers, descendants, and brothers” grammatically to “all,” meaning that some relatives were favored.
rows.anchor:
فقال الزمخشري:
عطفا على كلا بمعنى وفضلنا بعض آبائهم،

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya instead takes the phrase as a partitive selection of relatives whom God guided, whether prophets or other believers; the groups include ancestors, believing descendants, and Joseph's brothers.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: وهدينا من آبائهم وذرياتهم وإخوانهم جماعات فمن للتبعيض

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn Ka'b includes maternal uncles and aunts within “fathers” and therefore places Jesus under the expression through his mother.
rows.anchor: ولهذا قال محمد بن كعب: الخال والخالة انتهى،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We chose them and guided them” restates the earlier guidance to clarify that it is guidance to the straight, unbent path of God's unity and freedom from shirk.
rows.anchor: وكرر الهداية على سبيل التوضيح للهداية السابقة، وأنها هداية إلى طريق الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “That is God's guidance” identifies the straight-path guidance as God's and shows that guidance depends on His will; Ibn Atiyya instead points “that” back to the blessing of choosing them.
rows.anchor: ذلك الهدى إلى الطريق المستقيم هو هدى الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even people of this rank would lose all their deeds if they committed shirk; the conditional also confirms that the guidance just described is monotheism.
rows.anchor: ولو أشركوا مع فضلهم وتقدمهم وما رفع لهم من الدرجات لكانوا كغيرهم في حبوط أعمالهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The book, judgment, and prophethood are blessings distinguishing the selected prophets; “book” can mean the revealed scriptures, and “judgment” wisdom, adjudication, revealed law, understanding scripture, or religious jurisprudence.
rows.anchor: والكتاب: جنس للكتب الإلهية كصحف إبراهيم والتوراة والزبور والإنجيل،

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi describes book-giving as rank of knowledge, judgment as effective rule over outward matters, and prophethood as the rank from which both other ranks follow.
rows.anchor: آتيناهم الكتاب هي رتبة العلم يحكمون بها على بواطن الناس وأرواحهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “if these disbelieve in it” may refer to prophethood as the nearest antecedent or to all three gifts; “these” refers to the Quraysh and other unbelievers of that era.
rows.anchor: الظاهر أن الضمير في بها عائد إلى النبوة لأنها أقرب مذكور

rows.speaker: أبو رجاء
rows.claim: The people entrusted to believe in the revelation are identified variously as angels, believers of Medina, earlier prophets and their followers, the eighteen named prophets, the Emigrants and Helpers, all believers, or Persians; Abu Hayyan says the meaning extends to believers and disbelievers through the end of time.
rows.anchor: والقوم الموكلون بها هنا هم الملائكة قاله أبو رجاء، أو مؤمنو أهل المدينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Those whom God guided” points to the previously named prophets; the command is to follow their monotheism and fundamentals of faith, not their differing or abrogated legal systems.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الاقتداء في الصبر كما صبر من قبله،

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya allows “those” to point instead to the people entrusted with the prior revelation, where some interpretations of that group permit the reference.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن تكون الإشارة بأولئك إلى قوما وذلك يترتب على بعض التأويلات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other views take the command as emulating the prophets' patience, following all their guidance unless evidence excludes it, or adopting their virtues; one list enumerates their distinct moral excellences, all united in Muhammad.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الاقتداء في الصبر كما صبر من قبله،

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari reads the fronted “their guidance” as exclusive, a grammatical argument Abu Hayyan rejects as he does its use in “You alone we worship.”
rows.anchor: فبهداهم اقتده فاختص هداهم بالاقتداء ولا يقتدى إلا بهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The readings of “follow it” vary: the Hijazi readers and Abu Amr retain a silent hāʾ in connection and pause; the Kufans drop it in connection; Hisham partially vowels it; Ibn Dhakwan connects it with yāʾ, parsed as a pronoun rather than pause hāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحرميان وأهل حرميهما وأبو عمرو اقتده بالهاء ساكنة وصلا ووقفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan rejects Ibn Mujahid's condemnation of the kasra reading and says the alternative analysis of the letter as a pause hāʾ is weak.
rows.anchor: وتغليظ ابن مجاهد قراءة الكسر غلط منه وتأويلها على أنها هاء السكت ضعيف

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid identifies the people entrusted with the revelation as Persians.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: هم الفرس والآية وإن كان قد فسر بها مخصوصون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet asks no payment for calling people to the Qur'an, guidance, and straight path; the Qur'an is an admonition for all peoples.
rows.anchor: أي على الدعاء إلى القرآن وهو الهدى والصراط المستقيم. أجرا أي أجرة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The claim that God sent nothing to any human is attributed to the Jews, with a specific account placing it in the mouth of the Jewish scholar Malik ibn al-Sayf.
rows.anchor: نزلت في اليهود قاله ابن عباس ومحمد بن كعب، أو في مالك بن الصيف اليهودي

rows.speaker: مالك بن الصيف
rows.claim: In the report, the Prophet adjures Malik by the one who revealed the Torah and asks whether it says God dislikes the fat rabbi; Malik says yes, is told that he is that rabbi, becomes angry, and denies revelation to any human.
rows.anchor:
مالك بن الصيف اليهودي إذ
قال له الرسول: «أنشدك بالله

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi identifies the denier as the Jewish figure Fanhās ibn ʿĀzūrā.
rows.anchor: أو في فنحاص بن عازورا منهم قاله السدي

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the verse concerns Jews and Christians, whereas Mujahid and others apply it to Arab polytheists; one transmission from Mujahid specifies Quraysh.
rows.anchor: أو في اليهود والنصارى قاله قتادة، أو في مشركي العرب قاله مجاهد، وغيره،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root first means estimating an amount and extends to knowing a thing’s measure; the cited phrase about a cloudy moon means seeking to determine its course.
rows.anchor: وأصل القدر معرفة الكمية يقال: قدر الشيء إذا حزره وسبره

rows.speaker: الماتريدي
rows.claim: Al-Maturidi asks who can exalt or know God fully, then cites the angels’ confession that they did not worship Him as due and the Prophet’s inability to enumerate praise.
rows.anchor: قال الماتريدي: ومن الذي يعظم الله حق عظمته أو يعرفه حق معرفته؟

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: The Prophet says he cannot enumerate praise of God; Abu Hayyan allows the phrase to mean that people failed to exalt Him to the limit of their capacity.
rows.anchor: «لا أحصي ثناء عليك» وينفصل عن هذا

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: Abu al-Aliya, followed by al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, says they failed to describe God as befits what is necessary, impossible, and possible for Him.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو العالية: واختاره الخليل بن أحمد معناه: ما وصفوه حق صفته

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas also explains the phrase as failure to believe in God as He deserves and to know that He can do all things.
rows.anchor: ما آمنوا بالله حق إيمانه وعلموا أن الله على كل شيء قدير

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda also glosses it as failing to worship God as He deserves; another gloss equates it with failing to revere Him properly.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة أيضا: ما عبدوه حق عبادته، وقيل: ما أجلوه

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya sees a general failure to assess God properly, but says the following claim about revelation makes ignorance of God and denial of messengers the immediate implication.
rows.anchor: من توفية القدر فهي عامة يدخل تحتها من لم يعرف ومن لم يعظم وغير ذلك

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says the deniers failed to recognize God's mercy and kindness in sending messengers, or His anger and power toward those bold enough to deny prophethood; he identifies the speakers as Jews from the readings addressing them directly.
rows.anchor: ما عرفوا الله حق معرفته في الرحمة على عباده واللطف بهم حين أنكروا بعثة الرسل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The identity of the speakers follows the disputed occasion of revelation; if the verse concerns Israelites, it must be Medinan, as al-Naqqash reports.
rows.anchor: والضمير في وما قدروا عائد على من أنزلت الآية بسببه على الخلاف السابق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and Isa al-Thaqafi read the verb with a doubled qāf and fatḥa on dāl; “rightly” is a cognate accusative, and Ibn Atiyya's comment suggests “when” may express cause.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وعيسى الثقفي وما قدروا بالتشديد حق قدره بفتح الدال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the deniers are Israelites, the rebuttal is direct; if they are Arabs, the Torah’s revelation to Moses is a widely transmitted fact they do not reject.
rows.anchor: إن كان المنكرون بني إسرائيل فالاحتجاج عليهم واضح لأنهم ملتزمون نزول الكتاب على موسى

rows.speaker: أبو حامد الغزالي
rows.claim: Al-Ghazali analyzes the rebuttal as a second-figure syllogism and reductio: if no human received revelation, Moses could not be human, an impossible conclusion; Abu Hayyan draws the broader point that contradiction exposes an argument's falsity.
rows.anchor: هذه الآية مبنية على الشكل الثاني من الأشكال المنطقية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ghazali analyzes the rebuttal as a syllogism and reductio: if no human received revelation, Moses could not have been human, an impossible conclusion.
rows.anchor: هذه الآية مبنية على الشكل الثاني من الأشكال المنطقية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the majority reading with second-person verbs, God reproaches Israelites for turning the Torah into sheets so they could display some passages and conceal others, including signs of Muhammad's mission.
rows.anchor: وظاهره أنه لبني إسرائيل والمعنى: تجعلونه ذا قراطيس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The charge condemns their distortion and selective disclosure of the book Moses brought as light and guidance; second-person agreement continues the address “you knew.”
rows.anchor: وتتناسق قراءة التاء مع قوله: علمتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the deniers are Arabs, taking the verbs as direct address to Jews abruptly changes interlocutors and disrupts the sentence; the alternative is to see the shared rejection of Muhammad as allowing shifts between Arabs and Israelites.
rows.anchor: لأن فيه تفكيكا لنظم الآية وتركيبها، حيث جعل الكلام أولا خطابا مع الكفار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read all three verbs in the third person instead of directly addressing the Israelites.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير وأبو عمرو بالياء على الغيبة في الثلاثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “You learned what neither you nor your ancestors knew” may address Israelites to acknowledge or condemn their learning, Arabs as a blessing of guidance, believing Jews, or believing Quraysh; what they learned may be Torah, Islam, its laws, or Qur'an.
rows.anchor: ظاهره أنه خطاب لبني إسرائيل مقصود به الامتنان عليهم وعلى آبائهم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari takes the address as Jews: through Muhammad they learned revelation unknown even to their learned ancestors, including the Qur'an's resolution of Israelite disputes.
rows.anchor: الخطاب لليهود أي علمتم على لسان محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم مما أوحي إليه ما لم تعلموا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The book is the Torah, and “light and guidance” are circumstantial descriptions governed by either “sent down” or “brought.”
rows.anchor: والكتاب هنا التوراة وانتصب نورا وهدى على الحال والعامل أنزل أو جاء.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Say: God” commands a direct answer because the opponents cannot deny that a book marked by light, guidance, and miracles has God as its sender; Ibn Atiyya's hypothetical need to answer confused questioners is unnecessary.
rows.anchor: أمره بالمبادرة إلى الجواب أي قل الله أنزله فإنهم لا يقدرون أن يناكروك

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya alternatively supplies a situation in which they are ignorant, confused, or asking, but Abu Hayyan says no such premise is needed.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون المعنى فإن جهلوا أو تحيروا أو سألوا ونحو هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Leave them in their vain discourse, playing” tells the Prophet to let them continue useless talk; “playing” may modify them or their diversion, and “in their diversion” attaches in several grammatical ways.
rows.anchor: أي في باطلهم الذي يخوضون فيه ويقال لمن كان في عمل لا يجدي عليه إنما أنت لاعب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If “leave them” is a truce, fighting verses abrogate it; if it is a threat or warning rather than a truce, there is no abrogation.
rows.anchor: وظاهر الأمر أنه موادعة فيكون منسوخا بآيات القتال وإن جعل تهديدا أو وعيدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After establishing revelation against deniers, the passage declares this revealed Qur'an blessed and beneficial; the mention of blessing reinforces an already entailed property of revelation, while the wording foregrounds the contested act of sending it down.
rows.anchor: وهذا القرآن لما ذكر وقرر أن إنكار من أنكر أن يكون الله أنزل على بشر شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “a blessed reminder We sent down” elsewhere follows the mention of Moses' criterion, light, and reminder; “sent down” describes a renewed act, while “blessed” names an enduring quality.
rows.anchor: ولما كان الإنزال يتجدد عبر بالوصف الذي هو فعل، ولما كان وصفه بالبركة وصفا لا يفارق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A final alternative makes the address those Quraysh believers whom the Messenger was sent to warn, not Israelites.
rows.anchor: الخطاب لمن آمن من قريش لتنذر قوما ما أنذر آباؤهم انتهى.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Confirming what came before it” refers either to God's revealed books generally or specifically to the Torah; Ibn Atiyya rejects the resurrection interpretation because the Qur'an precedes the Resurrection.
rows.anchor: مصدق الذي بين يديه أي من كتب الله المنزلة، وقيل التوراة، وقيل البعث،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Mother of Cities is Mecca, named for its role in the origin and spread of religion, its centrality, its status as qibla and pilgrimage site, and the first house established for people.
rows.anchor: أم القرى مكة وسميت بذلك لأنها منشأ الدين ودحو الأرض منها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas takes “those around it” to mean all people of the earth; another view narrows them to Arabs, which some Jews used to claim Muhammad's mission was limited to Arabia.
rows.anchor: أم القرى ومن حولها طائفة من اليهود زعموا أنه رسول إلى العرب فقط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan answers the claim of an Arab-only mission: “around it” can cover the whole world, and even a geographically narrow sense would not exclude others except by a weak argument from implication.
rows.anchor: وأجيب بأن ومن حولها عام في جميع الأرض ولو فرضنا الخصوص لم يكن في ذكر جزيرة العرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The people of the Mother of Cities” omits “people,” since buildings cannot be warned, like “ask the town”; “around it” remains an adverb and cannot be used as a direct object.
rows.anchor: وحذف أهل الدلالة المعنى عليه لأن الأبنية لا تنذر كقوله: وسئل القرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Bakr reads “that it may warn” with the Qur'an as subject, while the majority read “that you may warn” addressing the Prophet; al-Zamakhshari connects the purpose clause to the book's description.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو بكر لينذر أي القرآن بمواعظه وأوامره، وقرأ الجمهور ولتنذر خطابا للرسول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “believe in it” apparently refers to the book: those who believe in resurrection accept a revelation rich in judgment and promises; belief in resurrection entails the other articles of faith and motivates religious fear. It may instead refer to the Messenger.
rows.anchor: الظاهر أن الضمير في به عائد على الكتاب أي الذين يصدقون بأن لهم حشرا ونشرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer is singled out as religion's pillar and the noblest worship after belief; maintaining it means regular, timely, proper performance. The word “faith” can refer to prayer, and abandoning it is described as unbelief.
rows.anchor: خص الصلاة لأنها عماد الدين ومن حافظ عليها كان محافظا على أخواتها

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: A report says that whoever deliberately abandons prayer has disbelieved; Abu Hayyan gives no grading for it here.
rows.anchor: من ترك الصلاة متعمدا فقد كفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers use the singular “their prayer” generically; a transmission by Khalaf from Yahya from Abu Bakr uniquely has the plural form.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور على صلاتهم بالتوحيد والمراد به الجنس

rows.speaker: الزهراوي
rows.claim: Al-Zahrawi and al-Mahdawi say the threat concerns al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and perhaps fellow mockers, who parodied Qurʾanic style with absurd verses about sowing, baking, cooking, grinding, and eating.
rows.anchor: ذكر الزهراوي والمهدوي إن الآية نزلت في النضر بن الحارث قيل: وفي المستهزئين معه

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada and others identify the targets as Musaylima al-Hanafi and al-Aswad al-Ansi, citing a report of the Prophet seeing two bracelets.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة وغيره: المراد بها مسيلمة الحنفي والأسود العنسي

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari identifies the claimant as either Musaylima or the liar of Sanaʾa, al-Aswad al-Ansi.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: وهو مسيلمة الحنفي أو كذاب صنعاء الأسود العنسي

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says the verse concerns Abd Allah ibn Saʿd ibn Abi Sarh, who marveled at a creation passage, inserted “Blessed is God, the best of creators,” and then claimed he could produce revelation like it.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: المراد بها عبد الله بن سعد بن أبي سرح العامري

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima assigns the verse's first part to Musaylima and its final claim to Ibn Abi Sarh; he also reports that Ibn Abi Sarh substituted other divine attributes while dictating.
rows.anchor: أولها في مسيلمة وآخرها في ابن أبي سرح

rows.speaker: شرحبيل بن سعد
rows.claim: Shurahbil ibn Sa'd says it was revealed about Ibn Abi Sarh, who apostatized, hid during the Meccan conquest, and was ultimately protected after Uthman interceded with the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وقال شرحبيل بن سعد: نزلت في ابن أبي سرح ومن قال: سأنزل مثل ما أنزل الله ارتد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage warns pretenders after describing the blessed Qur'an. Its sequence moves from general fabrication, to a false revelation claim, to the narrower claim of composing something like Qur'an; repeated “whoever” marks different referents, and “I will send down” is a false promise and metaphor for composing imitation.
rows.anchor: وبدأ أولا بالعام وهو افتراء الكذب على الله وهو أعم من أن يكون ذلك الافتراء بادعاء وحي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Ibn Abi Sarh account means “like what you claim God sent down,” not that the claimant believed God had sent anything down; Abu Hayya reads the phrase with a doubled zāy in one reading.
rows.anchor: ليس معتقده أن الله أنزل شيئا وإنما المعنى مثل ما أنزل الله على زعمكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although tied to named people, the threat applies to every false prophet, including Tulayha, al-Mukhtar, Sajah, and later claimants; Abu Hayyan recounts two later examples, one executed and one dismissed as foolish.
rows.anchor: وهذه الآية وإن كان سبب نزولها في مخصوصين فهي شاملة لكل من ادعى مثل دعواهم
